[[File:Chandrasekhar's H-function.jpg|thumb|Chandrasekhar's ''H''-function for different albedo]]
{{DISPLAYTITLE:Chandrasekhar's ''H''-function}}
In atmospheric [[radiation]], '''Chandrasekhar's ''H''-function''' appears as the solutions of problems involving scattering, introduced by the [[Indian American]] [[astrophysicist]] [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]].<ref>Chandrasekhar, Subrahmanyan. Radiative transfer. Courier Corporation, 2013.</ref><ref>Howell, John R., M. Pinar Menguc, and Robert Siegel. Thermal radiation heat transfer. CRC press, 2010.</ref><ref>[[Modest, Michael F.]] Radiative heat transfer. Academic press, 2013.</ref><ref>Hottel, Hoyt Clarke, and Adel F. Sarofim. Radiative transfer. McGraw-Hill, 1967.</ref><ref>Sparrow, Ephraim M., and Robert D. Cess. "Radiation heat transfer." Series in Thermal and Fluids Engineering, New York: McGraw-Hill, 1978, Augmented ed. (1978).</ref> The Chandrasekhar's ''H''-function <math>H(\mu)</math> defined in the interval <math>0\leq\mu\leq 1</math>, satisfies the following nonlinear integral equation

:<math>H(\mu) = 1+\mu H(\mu)\int_0^1 \frac{\Psi(\mu')}{\mu + \mu'}H(\mu') \, d\mu'</math>

where the characteristic function <math>\Psi(\mu)</math> is an even polynomial in <math>\mu</math> satisfying the following condition

:<math>\int_0^1\Psi(\mu) \, d\mu \leq \frac{1}{2}</math>.

If the equality is satisfied in the above condition, it is called ''conservative case'', otherwise ''non-conservative''. [[Albedo]] is given by <math>\omega_o= 2\Psi(\mu) = \text{constant}</math>. An alternate form which would be more useful in calculating the ''H'' function numerically by iteration was derived by Chandrasekhar as,

: <math>\frac{1}{H(\mu)} = \left[1-2\int_0^1\Psi(\mu) \, d\mu\right]^{1/2} + \int_0^1 \frac{\mu'\Psi(\mu')}{\mu + \mu'}H(\mu') \, d\mu'</math>.

In conservative case, the above equation reduces to 

:<math>\frac{1}{H(\mu)}= \int_0^1 \frac{\mu' \Psi(\mu')}{\mu+\mu'}H(\mu')d\mu'</math>.

==Approximation==

The ''H'' function can be approximated up to an order <math>n</math> as

: <math>H(\mu) = \frac{1}{\mu_1 \cdots \mu_n}\frac{\prod_{i=1}^n (\mu+\mu_i)}{\prod_\alpha (1+k_\alpha\mu)}</math>

where <math>\mu_i</math> are the zeros of [[Legendre polynomials]] <math>P_{2n}</math> and <math>k_\alpha</math> are the positive, non vanishing roots of the associated characteristic equation

:<math>1 = 2 \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{a_j\Psi(\mu_j)}{1-k^2\mu_j^2}</math>

where <math>a_j</math> are the quadrature weights given by

:<math>a_j = \frac{1}{P_{2n}'(\mu_j)}\int_{-1}^1 \frac{P_{2n}(\mu_j)}{\mu-\mu_j} \, d\mu_j</math>

==Explicit solution in the complex plane==
In complex variable <math>z</math> the ''H'' equation is 

: <math> H(z) = 1- \int_0^1 \frac z {z+\mu} H(\mu)\Psi(\mu) \, d\mu, \quad \int_0^1 |\Psi(\mu)| \, d\mu \leq \frac{1}{2}, \quad \int_0^\delta |\Psi(\mu)| \, d\mu \rightarrow 0, \ \delta\rightarrow 0</math>

then for <math>\Re (z)>0</math>, a unique solution is given by

:<math>\ln H(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{-i\infty}^{+ i\infty} \ln T(w) \frac{z}{w^2-z^2} \, dw</math>

where the imaginary part of the function <math>T(z)</math> can vanish if <math>z^2</math> is real i.e., <math>z^2 = u+iv = u\ (v=0)</math>. Then we have

: <math>T(z) = 1- 2 \int_0^1 \Psi(\mu) \, d\mu - 2 \int_0^1 \frac{\mu^2 \Psi(\mu)}{u-\mu^2} \, d\mu</math>

The above solution is unique and bounded in the interval <math>0\leq z\leq 1</math> for conservative cases. In non-conservative cases, if the equation <math>T(z)=0</math> admits the roots <math>\pm 1/k</math>, then there is a further solution given by

:<math>H_1(z) = H(z) \frac{1+kz}{1-kz}</math>

==Properties==

*<math>\int_0^1 H(\mu)\Psi(\mu) \, d\mu = 1-\left[1-2\int_0^1\Psi(\mu) \, d\mu \right]^{1/2}</math>. For conservative case, this reduces to <math>\int_0^1 \Psi(\mu)d\mu=\frac{1}{2}</math>.
*<math>\left[1-2\int_0^1\Psi(\mu) \, d\mu\right]^{1/2} \int_0^1 H(\mu) \Psi(\mu) \mu^2 \, d\mu + \frac{1}{2} \left[\int_0^1 H(\mu)\Psi(\mu)\mu \, d\mu\right]^2 = \int_0^1 \Psi(\mu)\mu^2 \, d\mu</math>. For conservative case, this reduces to <math>\int_0^1 H(\mu)\Psi(\mu) \mu d\mu = \left[2\int_0^1 \Psi(\mu)\mu^2d\mu\right]^{1/2}</math>.
*If the characteristic function is <math>\Psi(\mu)=a+b\mu^2</math>, where <math>a, b </math> are two constants(have to satisfy <math>a+b/3\leq 1/2</math>) and if <math>\alpha_n = \int_0^1 H(\mu)\mu^n \, d\mu, \ n\geq 1</math> is the nth moment of the ''H'' function, then we have 
:<math>\alpha_0 = 1 + \frac{1}{2} (a\alpha_0^2 + b \alpha_1^2)</math>
and
:<math>(a+b\mu^2) \int_0^1\frac{H(\mu')}{\mu+\mu'}\,d\mu'=\frac{H(\mu)-1}{\mu H(\mu)}-b(\alpha_1-\mu\alpha_0)</math>
